cards.front: In striated muscle, many tiny {{c1::sarcomere}} shortenings in a row add up to one visible pull.
cards.back: A muscle can only pull; it cannot push.
cards.quote: In striated muscle, many tiny sarcomere shortenings in a row add up to one visible pull.

cards.front: In a skeletal muscle sarcomere, what do the A band, the I band and the H zone each correspond to?
cards.back: A band: the length of the thick filaments. I band: thin filament with no thick filament beside it (straddles the Z disc). H zone: thick filament with no thin filament beside it.
cards.quote: The A band is the length of the thick filaments.
cards.section: From nerve to calcium to cross-bridge

cards.front: As a skeletal muscle sarcomere shortens, which regions narrow, which keeps its width, and why?
cards.back: The I band and H zone narrow; the A band keeps its width. The filaments do not shorten; they slide, so overlap grows (the sliding filament model).
cards.quote: As overlap grows, the I band and H zone narrow and the A band keeps its width
cards.section: From nerve to calcium to cross-bridge

cards.front: Two fully activated muscles have the same fibre type, cross-section and load, but one is twice as long, with twice as many sarcomeres in series. Which pulls harder, and which shortens farther and faster?
cards.back: They pull equally hard. The longer one shortens twice as far in the same time, so twice as fast.
cards.why: Sarcomeres in series pass the same force along like chain links, but each adds its own shortening. Force depends on filaments side by side, set by cross-section.
cards.quote: Force depends instead on how many filaments lie side by side, set by the cross-section across the fibres.
cards.section: From nerve to calcium to cross-bridge

cards.front: Trace the steps from a motor neuron impulse to calcium release in a vertebrate skeletal muscle fibre.
cards.back: Acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction depolarizes the fibre; an action potential runs along the membrane and down T tubules; a voltage sensor opens the SR calcium release channel; calcium floods out.
cards.quote: the neuron releases acetylcholine, which opens channels in the fibre's membrane and depolarizes it
cards.section: From nerve to calcium to cross-bridge

cards.front: Does vertebrate skeletal muscle need calcium entering from outside the cell to release calcium from its sarcoplasmic reticulum? Why?
cards.back: No. A voltage sensor in the T-tubule membrane (CaV1.1) is linked to the SR release channel (RyR1) and opens it when the voltage changes.
cards.quote: Calcium entering from outside the cell is not required for this step; that is where the heart differs (below).
cards.section: From nerve to calcium to cross-bridge

cards.front: How does calcium switch on the thin filament of vertebrate skeletal muscle?
cards.back: Calcium binds troponin (at troponin C), which rolls tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads can attach as cross-bridges.
cards.quote: is a complex of three proteins on the thin filament, with calcium binding at troponin C
cards.section: From nerve to calcium to cross-bridge

cards.front: What are the two jobs of ATP in skeletal muscle contraction?
cards.back: First, releasing and re-cocking each myosin head. Second, relaxation: SR pumps use ATP to move calcium back into the store, so tropomyosin covers the binding sites again.
cards.quote: Its second is relaxation: SR pumps use ATP to move calcium back into the store
cards.section: From nerve to calcium to cross-bridge

cards.front: A drug blocks the calcium pumps of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in a skeletal muscle fibre, while ATP stays available. After a stimulus, what happens to relaxation, and why?
cards.back: Relaxation fails or is greatly slowed: calcium stays high in the cytoplasm, so tropomyosin stays off the binding sites and cross-bridges keep cycling.
cards.why: Relaxation depends on ATP-driven pumps returning calcium to the SR.
cards.quote: tropomyosin covers the sites again, and the muscle relaxes
cards.section: From nerve to calcium to cross-bridge

cards.front: A skeletal muscle fibre runs completely out of ATP while many myosin heads are attached to actin. What state does the fibre enter, and why?
cards.back: It becomes stiff and locked: attached heads cannot let go of actin.
cards.why: ATP's first job is releasing and re-cocking each myosin head; without ATP the attached cross-bridges stay attached.
cards.quote: myosin heads use ATP to drag actin filaments past them, and calcium switches the sliding on

cards.front: What is a motor unit, and how does skeletal muscle grade its force?
cards.back: A motor neuron and the muscle fibres it drives. Force is graded by how many motor units fire and how often.
cards.quote: Graded force comes from how many motor units (a motor neuron and the fibres it drives) fire and how often
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: What starts each heartbeat, and how does excitation spread through cardiac muscle?
cards.back: Pacemaker cells generate action potentials on their own (no motor neuron); gap junctions joining the short, branched cells let current pass cell to cell, so a wave spreads. Nerves adjust rate and force.
cards.quote: No motor neuron starts the beat: pacemaker cells generate action potentials on their own
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: What is calcium-induced calcium release in mammalian heart cells?
cards.back: Calcium entering through membrane channels during the action potential triggers a much larger release of calcium from the SR.
cards.quote: In mammalian heart cells, calcium entering through membrane channels during the action potential triggers a much larger release from the SR.
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: Heart cells from adult rat ventricles have their surface membrane removed (skinned). A small controlled rise in bath calcium triggers calcium release from the SR. What does this show?
cards.back: Calcium itself can trigger SR calcium release, key evidence for calcium-induced calcium release in mammalian heart cells.
cards.why: With the membrane removed, the trigger cannot be a membrane voltage change; only the calcium rise was applied.
cards.quote: a small controlled rise in bath calcium triggered calcium release from the SR
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: Why does smooth muscle have no stripes, and what controls it?
cards.back: Its actin and myosin are not organized into sarcomeres. It is involuntary: autonomic nerves, hormones and stretch act on it.
cards.quote: Its actin and myosin are not organized into sarcomeres, so it has no stripes.
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: How does a rise in calcium switch on smooth muscle?
cards.back: Calcium binds calmodulin; calcium-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase, which phosphorylates the myosin light chain and turns myosin on. The switch is on myosin, not troponin.
cards.quote: Calcium binds calmodulin, and calcium-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: Purified smooth muscle myosin is phosphorylated on its light chain, and its actin-activated ATPase activity rises; removing the phosphate lowers it. What does this show?
cards.back: Light-chain phosphorylation is the on switch for smooth muscle myosin: it raises the rate at which myosin splits ATP with actin present.
cards.quote: this phosphate raised the myosin's actin-activated ATPase activity (its rate of splitting ATP with actin present)
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: A drug inhibits the phosphatase that removes phosphate from the myosin light chain in vascular smooth muscle. Calcium then falls. Predict the effect on the vessel.
cards.back: The muscle stays contracted longer and the vessel stays narrowed: myosin keeps its phosphate and stays on.
cards.why: As calcium falls the kinase slows, but relaxation needs the phosphatase to take the phosphate off.
cards.quote: takes the phosphate off, so the muscle generally relaxes
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: A toxin prevents calcium from binding troponin C. Predict its effect on vertebrate skeletal muscle and on smooth muscle.
cards.back: Skeletal muscle cannot contract, because tropomyosin stays over the binding sites. Smooth muscle still contracts, because its switch is calcium-calmodulin acting on myosin.
cards.quote: Smooth muscle has no troponin switch; its switch is on myosin.
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: A toxin closes all gap junctions. Predict the effect on vertebrate skeletal muscle and on the heart.
cards.back: Skeletal muscle is largely unaffected; the heart's wave of excitation cannot spread from cell to cell, so its cells no longer beat together.
cards.why: Each skeletal fibre is driven by its own motor neuron and is not electrically coupled; cardiac cells rely on gap junctions.
cards.quote: Each fibre contracts when its own motor neuron fires, and fibres are not electrically connected to each other.
cards.section: Three muscles, three triggers

cards.front: How do oxidative and glycolytic skeletal muscle fibres differ in how they make ATP?
cards.back: Oxidative fibres make most ATP by aerobic respiration in mitochondria. Glycolytic fibres make ATP fast by glycolysis, which needs no oxygen, with less aerobic capacity.
cards.quote: Glycolytic fibres make ATP fast by glycolysis (glycolysis), which does not need oxygen
cards.section: Fast and slow: fibres, tuna and chickens

cards.front: Contrast slow oxidative and fast glycolytic skeletal fibres in speed, colour and fatigue.
cards.back: Slow oxidative: slow, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, dark red, fatigue-resistant. Fast glycolytic: fast, pale, fatigue sooner. (Fast oxidative: fast but mainly aerobic.)
cards.quote: Slow oxidative fibres contract slowly, are rich in mitochondria and in myoglobin
cards.section: Fast and slow: fibres, tuna and chickens

cards.front: A domestic chicken stands and walks all day but flaps its wings only in brief bursts. Predict which muscles are darker and which are pale.
cards.back: Leg muscles are darker; breast (flight) muscles are pale.
cards.why: Muscles used for steady work are red and oxidative; those used for bursts are pale and glycolytic.
cards.quote: The leg muscles used in standing and walking are darker, and the breast muscles that power brief bursts of flapping are pale.
cards.section: Fast and slow: fibres, tuna and chickens

cards.front: A drug changes the behaviour of IIb fibres in rats. Can you assume it will act the same way on human fibres labelled IIb by staining?
cards.back: No. Human fibres long labelled IIb express mostly IIx myosin, not the rodent IIb isoform, so rodent IIb results cannot be read straight across.
cards.quote: Human fibres long labelled IIb by staining express mostly IIx myosin, not the rodent IIb isoform
cards.section: Fibre names depend on the species

cards.front: A fish with a thin red band of muscle along each side and a large mass of white muscle is placed in water low in oxygen. Which of its muscles depend on oxygen to make ATP, and which kind of sustained swimming do they power?
cards.back: The red (oxidative) muscle depends on oxygen, because it makes most ATP by aerobic respiration; it powers sustained cruising. The white (glycolytic) muscle makes ATP by glycolysis, which needs no oxygen, and powers brief bursts.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that oxidative fibres need oxygen and glycolytic fibres do not.
cards.quote: Oxidative fibres make most of their ATP with oxygen, by aerobic respiration in mitochondria.
cards.section: Fast and slow: fibres, tuna and chickens

cards.front: Why must stretch-activated force in asynchronous flight muscle rise after a delay rather than instantly?
cards.back: Instant force would act like a stiffer spring and add no net work, so the beat would die away. The delay lets force peak while a set shortens, so each set does work on the thorax and stretches its partner.
cards.quote: The delay lets force peak while a set is shortening, so each set does work on the thorax
cards.section: A fly's wings outrun its nerves

cards.front: A tethered insect beats its wings at 200 beats per second, while its main flight muscles record 5 large spikes per second that are not timed to particular wingbeats. How many wingbeats per impulse, and what kind of flight muscle is this?
cards.back: 200 / 5 = 40 wingbeats per impulse. Many beats per impulse, not one to one, means asynchronous flight muscle.
cards.quote: The one-to-one rule is about the large spikes he linked to nerve impulses, so they are what break it.
cards.section: A fly's wings outrun its nerves

cards.front: What did Pringle's 1949 insect flight recordings show, and what did they leave unsettled?
cards.back: Large spikes far fewer than wingbeats; he only suggested a stretch response (stretch activation was reported in 1959). Unsettled: whether the spikes were propagated action potentials, and how the muscle oscillates.
cards.quote: In 1949 Pringle only suggested that the muscle responds to stretch
cards.section: A fly's wings outrun its nerves

cards.front: What is a hydrostatic skeleton? Give an example.
cards.back: Fluid under pressure in a closed cavity. An earthworm's body-wall muscles contract against fluid in its body cavity, so each segment can lengthen or shorten.
cards.quote: A hydrostatic skeleton is fluid under pressure in a closed cavity.
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: How does a muscular hydrostat, such as an octopus arm or a mammalian tongue, move without bone or a fluid cavity?
cards.back: It is mostly muscle at constant volume, so muscle in one direction acts against muscle in another.
cards.quote: octopus arms and mammalian tongues are mostly muscle at constant volume
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: Why must arthropods moult?
cards.back: Their exoskeleton is a hard outer case that cannot grow, so they shed it and make a larger one at each moult.
cards.quote: It cannot grow, so arthropods shed it and make a larger one at each moult
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: What two components make up bone matrix?
cards.back: Collagen fibres and a calcium phosphate mineral, hydroxyapatite.
cards.quote: Its matrix combines collagen fibres with a calcium phosphate mineral, hydroxyapatite.
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: Osteoblasts lay down new bone, {{c1::osteoclasts}} dissolve it, and osteocytes are former osteoblasts trapped in the matrix.
cards.quote: Osteoblasts lay down new bone, osteoclasts dissolve it, and osteocytes are former osteoblasts trapped in the matrix.
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: Why does a bone's shape change with the loads it carries?
cards.back: Bone is living tissue that is resorbed by osteoclasts and rebuilt by osteoblasts throughout life, so it remodels to its loads.
cards.quote: Because bone is resorbed and rebuilt throughout life, its shape changes with the loads it carries
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: Name the three structural classes of human joints, with an example of each where given.
cards.back: Fibrous (connective tissue, e.g. skull sutures), cartilaginous (joined by cartilage) and synovial (lubricated fluid-filled cavity, e.g. elbow and knee).
cards.quote: joints are grouped by structure as fibrous (bones joined by connective tissue, as in skull sutures)
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: Why do muscles at a synovial joint such as the elbow work in antagonistic groups?
cards.back: A muscle can only pull. Flexors (biceps, brachialis) bend the elbow, so a different muscle, the triceps, must pull to straighten it.
cards.quote: flexors such as the biceps and brachialis bend the elbow, and the triceps straightens it
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: In an idealized static model, a horizontal, weightless forearm holds a 25 N load 0.36 m from the elbow. The biceps alone pulls straight up with a moment arm of 0.045 m. What force does the biceps exert?
cards.back: Torques balance: F x 0.045 m = 25 N x 0.36 m = 9.0 N m, so F = 9.0 / 0.045 = 200 N, 8 times the load.
cards.quote: Each torque is a force times its moment arm, and the torques must balance
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: In an idealized forearm model, the load sits 0.30 m from the elbow and the biceps moment arm is 0.040 m. If the biceps shortens by 2.0 cm, about how far does the hand move (small angle)?
cards.back: Ratio 0.30 / 0.040 = 7.5, so the hand moves about 7.5 x 2.0 cm = 15 cm, and 7.5 times as fast.
cards.quote: the hand moves 0.30 / 0.040 = 7.5 times as far, and as fast, as the point where the biceps attaches
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: Why is the forearm with the biceps a third-class lever, and what does it trade?
cards.back: The muscle pulls between the pivot (elbow) and the load (hand). It gives up force for distance and speed.
cards.quote: This is a third-class lever: the muscle pulls between the pivot and the load, and gives up force for distance and speed.
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: In an idealized forearm model with a 20 N load 0.30 m from the elbow, the biceps moment arm is changed from 0.040 m to 0.060 m. What are the new biceps force and the new hand-to-insertion movement ratio, and what is traded?
cards.back: 20 x 0.30 = 6.0 N m; F = 6.0 / 0.060 = 100 N (down from 150 N). Ratio 0.30 / 0.060 = 5 (down from 7.5). Less force is needed, but the hand moves less far and less fast.
cards.why: Rests on torque balance: muscle force x muscle moment arm = load x load arm.
cards.quote: The biceps pulls straight up with a moment arm of 0.040 m, the perpendicular distance from the elbow to the line of the biceps' pull.
cards.section: Skeletons: water, armour and bone, with levers

cards.front: Frog skeletal fibres and mammalian (rat) ventricular cells are stimulated in normal solution, then in a calcium-free bath with a calcium binder. Predict force in each, and explain.
cards.back: Skeletal twitches continue for a time: the voltage sensor is linked mechanically to the SR release channel. Ventricular force falls quickly: entering calcium triggers SR release.
cards.quote: twitches continue for a time without calcium entry, because the voltage sensor is linked mechanically to the SR release channel
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a calcium-free bath experiment on muscle force, why record action potentials in every condition, and why return each preparation to normal solution?
cards.back: So a loss of force cannot be blamed on a membrane that no longer fires; and to show the effect reverses and the cells were undamaged.
cards.quote: Record action potentials in every condition, so that a loss of force cannot be blamed on a membrane that no longer fires.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An L-type calcium channel blocker reduces twitch force in frog skeletal fibres. Does this prove skeletal contraction needs calcium entry? What better test is there?
cards.back: No. In skeletal fibres the L-type channel (CaV1.1) is itself the voltage sensor, so a blocker can reduce force without any need for calcium entry. The calcium-free bath is the cleaner test.
cards.quote: there the L-type channel (CaV1.1) is itself the voltage sensor
cards.section: Reading the calcium-free test with care
